title: The Winning of a Sword: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Found a Noble Sword in a Wonderful Way, and How He Fought Again With It and Won That Battle._

As soon as the strange balsam had healed the terrible wounds King Arthur received in his battle with King Pellinore, he felt a strong desire to meet his enemy again. He wanted to try the fight once more and win back the honor he had lost. On the morning of the fourth day he was completely well. After he had eaten breakfast, he walked along the edge of the forest to refresh himself, listening to the woodbirds singing their morning songs as loudly as they could. Merlin walked beside him, and Arthur told Merlin that he meant to fight King Pellinore again. He said, “Merlin, it troubles me deeply that I came off so badly in my recent fight with King Pellinore. Truly, he is the best knight I have ever faced in all the world. Still, things might have gone differently if my sword had not broken and left me with no defense. However that may be, I want to try this adventure again, and I will do so as soon as I can.”

Merlin answered, “You are surely a brave man to be so eager for battle, when you came so close to death not even four days ago. But how can you hope to try this adventure without preparing? Look, you have no sword and no spear, and you do not even have your dagger to fight with. How can you hope to take on this adventure?”
King Arthur said, “That I do not know, but I will find some weapon as soon as I can. Even if I had nothing better than an oak club, I would still fight this battle again with a tool as poor as that.”

“Ha! My lord,” said Merlin, “I see that you are set on renewing this quarrel. So I will not try to stop you, but will do everything I can to help you get what you wish. To that end I must tell you about a part of this forest, which is a very strange place indeed. There is a woodland there that is sometimes called Arroy and sometimes the Forest of Adventure, because no knight ever enters it without some adventure coming to him. Close to Arroy lies a land of enchantment that has been seen several times. It is a wonderful land, for it holds a wide and spacious lake, and that lake is enchanted too. For some time now, people have seen what looks like a woman’s arm rising from the middle of that lake. The arm is very beautiful and is dressed in white silk, and its hand holds a sword so excellent and so lovely that no eye has ever seen its equal. The sword is called Excalibur, a name given to it by those who have seen it because of its marvelous brightness and beauty. Several knights have already seen that sword and tried to win it for themselves, but until now no one has been able to touch it, and many have lost their lives in the attempt. When anyone comes near it, he either sinks into the lake, or the arm vanishes completely, or it is pulled down beneath the water. That is why no one has ever been able to take that sword. Now, I can lead you to that Lake of Enchantment, and there you can see Excalibur with your own eyes. Once you have seen it, you may want to win it. If you can do that, you will have a sword well suited for fighting.”

“Merlin,” said the King, “this is a very strange thing you tell me. I want more than I can say to try to win this sword for myself, so I beg you to take me at once to this enchanted lake you speak of.” And Merlin said, “I will.”

So that morning King Arthur and Merlin said goodbye to the holy hermit, and the King knelt in the grass to receive his blessing. Then they left that place and went once more into the deeper forest, making their way to the part that was known as Arroy.

After a while they came to Arroy, and it was about noon. As they entered those woodlands they came to a small clearing, and there they saw a white doe with a golden collar around its neck. King Arthur said, “Look, Merlin, what a wonderful sight!” And Merlin said, “Let us follow that doe.” At this the doe turned, and they followed it. Before long they came to a gap in the trees where there was a small lawn of sweet, soft grass. There they saw a bower, and in front of the bower stood a table covered with a fine snow-white cloth and set with food: white bread, wine, and several kinds of meat. At the door of the bower stood a page dressed all in green. His hair was as black as ebony, and his eyes were as black as jet and very bright. When the page saw King Arthur and Merlin, he greeted them and welcomed the King warmly. He said, “Ha! King Arthur, you are welcome to this place. I beg you, get down from your horse and refresh yourself before going farther.”

King Arthur was unsure at first whether this might be some enchantment meant to harm him, for he was astonished that a page in the deep forest should know him so well. But Merlin told him to be of good cheer. He said, “Indeed, my lord, you may freely take this food, which I can tell you was prepared especially for you. What is more, you may take it as a sign that this adventure will end very happily.”

So King Arthur sat down at the table with a glad heart, for he was hungry. That page and another like him waited on him, serving all the food on silver plates and all the wine in golden goblets, just as he was used to being served in his own court. But these things were much more skillfully made, and more beautiful, than the tableware in the King’s court.

When he had eaten his fill, he washed his hands in a silver basin that the first page held out to him, and dried them on a fine linen napkin that the other page brought. Merlin refreshed himself too, and then they went on their way, delighted with this pleasant adventure. To the King it seemed to promise a good end to his undertaking.

About the middle of the afternoon King Arthur and Merlin suddenly came out of the forest onto a fair, level plain. It was covered with so many flowers that no one could imagine how many there were or how beautiful they were.

This was a wonderful land, for all the air seemed to be made of gold, it was so bright and shining. Here and there on the plain stood trees in full blossom, and their fragrance was so sweet that the King had never smelled anything like it. In the branches of those trees sat many birds of different colors, and their singing delighted the heart of anyone who heard it. In the middle of the plain lay a lake as bright as silver, and all around its edges grew great numbers of lilies and daffodils. Yet although the place was so lovely, there was not a single sign of human life anywhere. It seemed as lonely as the empty sky on a summer day. Because of the marvelous beauty of the place, and its strangeness and complete solitude, King Arthur understood that he must have come into a land of powerful enchantment. Happily, a fairy of very high rank lived there. A kind of fear wrapped around his spirit as he pushed his great milk-white war-horse through the long, fair grass dotted with flowers, and he did not know what strange things were about to happen to him.

When he reached the edge of the lake, he saw the wonder that Merlin had told him about. In the middle of the water was a beautiful arm, like a woman’s, dressed in white silk. Several bracelets of worked gold circled the arm, and the hand held a sword of marvelous workmanship up in the air above the water. Neither the arm nor the sword moved even a hair’s breadth. They were as still as a carved statue on the surface of the lake. The sun of that strange land shone down on the hilt of the sword, which was pure gold set with jewels of several kinds. The hilt and the bracelets on the arm glittered in the middle of the lake like a strange and splendid star. King Arthur sat on his war-horse and gazed from a distance at the arm and the sword, and he wondered greatly at them. But he did not know how he could reach the sword, for the lake was very wide and deep, and he could not tell how to get there and make the sword his own. As he sat thinking about this, he suddenly noticed a strange lady coming toward him through the tall flowers that bloomed along the shore. When he saw her, he quickly got down from his war-horse and went forward to meet her, with the bridle over his arm. When he came close to her, he saw that she was extraordinarily beautiful. Her face was as clear as wax, and her eyes were perfectly black, as bright and shining as two jewels set in ivory. Her hair was like silk, as black as black could be, and so long that it reached the ground as she walked. The lady was dressed all in green, except that a fine cord of crimson and gold was woven into the braids of her hair. Around her neck hung a lovely necklace of several strands of opals and emeralds set in skillfully worked gold, and around her wrists were bracelets of the same kind, opals and emeralds set in gold. When King Arthur saw her wonderful appearance, which was like an ivory statue of great beauty dressed in green, he at once knelt before her among all those flowers. He said, “Lady, I can plainly see that you are no mortal maiden, but one of the Fay. And I see that this place, because of its great beauty, can be nothing other than a land of Faerie that I have wandered into.”

And the Lady replied, “King Arthur, you speak truly, for I am indeed of Faerie. I may also tell you that my name is Nymue, and that I am the chief of those Ladies of the Lake you may have heard people speak of. You should know too that what you see over there as a wide lake is really a plain like this one, covered with flowers. In the middle of that plain stands a castle of white marble and deep blue, decorated with gold. But so that mortal eyes would not see our home, my sisters and I have spread the look of a lake over the whole castle, so that it is completely hidden. No mortal man can cross that lake except in one way, or he will surely die in it.”
“Lady,” said King Arthur, “what you tell me fills me with wonder. And I fear that in coming here I have done wrong to break in on the peace of your home.”

“No, not at all, King Arthur,” said the Lady of the Lake, “for truly you are very welcome here. I may also tell you that I feel more friendship for you and the noble knights of your court than you can easily guess. But I ask you, out of courtesy, to tell me what brings you to our land.”

“Lady,” said the King, “I will tell you the whole truth. Not long ago I fought a battle with a certain black knight, in which I was badly and painfully wounded. I broke my spear, snapped my sword, and even lost my dagger, so that I had no weapon left at all. In this need Merlin, here, told me about Excalibur, and how an arm in the middle of this magic lake always holds it up. So I came here and, behold, I find it just as he said. Now, Lady, if it is possible, I would gladly win that excellent sword, so that I could fight my battle to its end.”

“Ha! My lord King,” said the Lady of the Lake, “that sword is not easy to win, and I must tell you that several knights have lost their lives trying to do what you have in mind. Truly, no man can win that sword unless he is without fear and without reproach.”

“Alas, Lady!” said King Arthur, “that is sad news for me. Although I do not lack a knight’s courage, there are many things for which I blame myself. Still, I would gladly try this, even at great risk to myself. So I beg you, tell me how I can best take on this adventure.”

“King Arthur,” said the Lady of the Lake, “I will do what I have said to help you in this matter.” Then she lifted a single emerald that hung from a small golden chain at her belt, and the emerald was skillfully carved in the shape of a whistle. She put the whistle to her lips and blew on it sharply. At once something shining brightly appeared on the water, far away. It came toward them very fast, and as it drew near, it turned out to be a boat made entirely of carved brass. The front of the boat was carved in the shape of a beautiful woman’s head, and on each side were wings like a swan’s wings. The boat glided over the water like a swan, so swiftly that long lines like silver threads stretched out behind it across the water, which was otherwise as smooth as glass. When the brass boat reached the shore, it stopped there and did not move again.

Then the Lady of the Lake told King Arthur to get into the boat, and he did. As soon as he was aboard, the boat moved away from the shore as swiftly as it had come. Merlin and the Lady of the Lake stood at the water’s edge and watched King Arthur and the brass boat go.
King Arthur saw that the boat floated swiftly across the lake to the place where the arm held up the sword, and that the arm and the sword did not move but stayed just where they were.
Then King Arthur reached out and took the sword in his hand. At once the arm sank beneath the water, and King Arthur held the sword, with its scabbard and its belt, in his hand. They were his own.

Then his heart swelled with joy, as if it would burst inside his chest, for Excalibur was a hundred times more beautiful than he had thought possible. His heart nearly broke from pure happiness at having won that magic sword.

Then the brass boat carried him quickly back to land, and he stepped ashore where the Lady of the Lake and Merlin stood. Standing on the shore, he thanked the Lady beyond measure for all she had done to help him in his great undertaking, and she answered him with cheerful and gracious words.

Then King Arthur bowed to the lady, as was proper. He mounted his war-horse, and Merlin mounted his palfrey, and they rode away to go about their business. The King’s heart was still swelling with pure delight at having that beautiful sword for his own—the most beautiful and the most famous sword in all the world.

That night King Arthur and Merlin stayed with the holy hermit at his sanctuary in the forest. When morning came, the King bathed in the ice-cold forest fountain and felt wonderfully refreshed. Then they left, thanking the saintly man for the shelter he had given them.

Soon, around noon, they reached the valley of the Sable Knight. Everything was arranged exactly as it had been when King Arthur was there before: the gloomy castle, the lawn of smooth grass, the apple tree covered with shields, and the bridge where that single black shield hung.

“Now, Merlin,” said King Arthur, “this time I strictly forbid you to interfere in this quarrel. And if you value my favor, you must not use any of your magic on my behalf. So listen to what I say, and obey it with all possible care.”

Right away the King rode out onto the bridge. He seized the brass mallet and struck the black shield with all his strength. At once the portcullis of the castle dropped, just as before, and the Sable Knight rode out, already dressed and armed for the fight, as he had done the other time. He came to the head of the bridge, and King Arthur spoke to him like this: “Sir Pellinore, we know each other quite well now, and each of us believes he has a reason to quarrel with the other. You believe that I, for reasons of my own that seemed right to me, took away your kingly rank and drove you into this lonely forest. I believe that you set yourself up here to insult and harm knights, lords, and other people of my kingdom. So, since I am here as a wandering knight, I challenge you to fight me, man to man, until one of us has defeated the other.”

King Pellinore bowed his head in obedience at these words. Then he turned his horse, rode a short distance away, and took the place where he had stood before. King Arthur also rode a short distance away and took the place where he had stood before. At the same moment one of those tall pages dressed all in black and crimson came out of the castle. He gave King Arthur a good, sturdy spear of ash wood, well seasoned and not yet used in battle. When the two knights were ready, they shouted and drove their horses together. Each struck the other so squarely in the middle of his defenses that both spears shattered in their hands, bursting into small splinters as they had before.

Then each of the two knights skillfully leaped from his horse and drew his sword. They began to fight so fiercely and so violently that two wild bulls in the mountains could not have fought a more desperate battle.

But now that King Arthur had Excalibur to help him, he soon overcame his enemy. He gave King Pellinore several wounds and received none himself. Not a single drop of his blood was shed in that whole fight, though his enemy’s armor was soon stained crimson. At last King Arthur struck such a mighty blow that King Pellinore was stunned. His sword and shield dropped from his hands, his legs trembled beneath him, and he sank to his knees on the ground. Then he begged King Arthur for mercy, saying, “Spare my life and I will surrender to you.”

King Arthur said, “I will spare you, and I will do more than that. Now that you have surrendered to me, see! I will give back your power and your rank. I bear you no ill will, Pellinore. Still, I cannot tolerate rebels against my rule in this kingdom. As God is my judge, I declare that I think only of the good of the people of my kingdom. So whoever is against me is also against them, and whoever is against them is also against me. But now I will require a pledge of your good faith toward me in the future. You must send me your two eldest sons as hostages of your good will, namely Sir Aglaval and Sir Lamorack. Your young son, Dornar, you may keep with you for your comfort.”
So those two young knights came to the Court of King Arthur. They became very famous knights, and in time they were made fellows of the Round Table, with great honor.

King Arthur and King Pellinore went together into King Pellinore’s castle, and there King Pellinore’s wounds were bandaged and he was made comfortable. That night King Arthur stayed in King Pellinore’s castle. When morning came, he and Merlin went back to the King’s Court, which was waiting for him in the forest at the place where he had set it up.

King Arthur felt very great pleasure as he and Merlin rode back together through the forest. It was the leafiest time of the year, when the woodlands dressed themselves in their best clothes of clear, bright green. Every wooded hollow and little valley was full of the scent of the thickets. In every tangled depth the small birds sang with all their might, as though they would burst their little throats with the melody. The ground under the horses’ feet was so soft with fragrant moss that no sound of hoofbeats could be heard on the earth. The bright yellow sunlight came down through the leaves, so that the ground was scattered with a great many trembling circles like pure yellow gold. Now and then that sunlight would fall on the armed knight as he rode, so that his armor seemed to catch fire with a great glory, shining like a sudden bright star among the dark shadows of the woods.

So King Arthur took great joy in that forest land. He had no ache or pain of any kind, and his heart was lifted high by the wonderful success of the adventure he had undertaken. In that adventure he had not only turned a very bitter enemy into a friend who would be of great use and comfort to him, but he had also gained a sword like none the world had ever seen. Whenever he thought of that splendid sword hanging at his side, and whenever he remembered the land of Faëry he had wandered into and what had happened to him there, his heart filled with such pure joy that he hardly knew how to hold himself together. So great was the delight that filled his whole chest.

Indeed, I can think of no greater good to wish for you in all your life than that you might enjoy the happiness that comes to a person when he has done his very best and has completely succeeded in what he set out to do. Then all the world seems filled with a bright, shining light, and the body feels so lifted up that the feet are freed from heaviness and touch the earth very lightly, because of the lightness of the spirit within. So if it were in my power to give you the very best the world has to give, I would wish that you might win your battle as King Arthur won his battle at that time. I would wish that you might ride homeward in the same triumph and joy that filled him that day, and that the sunlight might shine around you as it shone around him. I would wish that the breezes might blow and all the little birds might sing with all their might as they sang for him, and that your heart might also sing its song of rejoicing in the pleasantness of the world in which you live.

As they rode through the forest together, Merlin said to the King, “My Lord, which would you rather have, Excalibur or the sheath that holds him?” King Arthur answered, “Ten thousand times I would rather have Excalibur than his sheath.” “In that you are wrong, my Lord,” said Merlin, “for let me tell you something. Excalibur is of such great temper that he can cut in two either a feather or a bar of iron. Yet his sheath is of such a kind that whoever wears it can suffer no wound in battle, and he cannot lose a single drop of blood. As proof, you may remember that in your recent battle with King Pellinore you suffered no wound and lost no blood.”

Then King Arthur turned a look of great displeasure on his companion and said, “Now, Merlin, I declare that you have taken from me all the glory of the battle I have just fought. What credit can there be for a knight who fights his enemy by means of enchantment such as you describe? Indeed, I am inclined to take this glorious sword back to that magic lake and throw it in, where it belongs. I believe a knight should fight by his own strength and not by magic.”

“My Lord,” said Merlin, “you are quite right in what you believe. But you must remember that you are not an ordinary wandering knight. You are a King, and your life does not belong to you but to your people. So you have no right to put it in danger, and you should do everything in your power to protect it. Therefore you should keep that sword, so that it may guard your life.”

Then King Arthur thought about those words in silence for a long while, and when he spoke it was like this: “Merlin, you are right in what you say. For the sake of my people, I will keep both Excalibur, to fight for them, and his sheath, to protect my life for their sake. Still, I will never use him again except in serious battle.” King Arthur kept to that promise, so that afterward he fought no mock battles except with a lance and on horseback.

King Arthur kept Excalibur as the greatest treasure of all his possessions. He said to himself, “A sword like this is fit for a king above other kings and a lord above other lords. God has seen fit to place that sword in my keeping in such a marvelous way, so He must mean for me to be His servant and do unusual things. Therefore I will treasure this noble weapon, not only for its excellent worth, but because it will be a sign to me of the great things that God, in His mercy, has plainly chosen me to do in His service.”

So King Arthur had a strong chest made for Excalibur. It was bound all around with many bands of wrought iron, studded all over with great iron nails, and locked with three great padlocks. In this strongbox he kept Excalibur lying on a cushion of crimson silk and wrapped in fine linen. Very few people ever saw the sword in its glory, except when it flashed like a sudden flame in the uproar of battle.

When the time came for King Arthur to defend his realm or his subjects against their enemies, he would take out the sword and fasten it at his side. When he did so, he looked like a hero of God wearing a blade of shining lightning. Yes, at such times Excalibur shone with such terrible brightness that the very sight of it would shake the spirit of every wrongdoer with such great fear that he would, in a way, feel the pangs of death before the edge of the blade ever touched his flesh.

So King Arthur treasured Excalibur, and the sword stayed with him all his life, so that the name of Arthur and the name of Excalibur are one. I believe that sword is the most famous of any that was ever seen or heard of in all the Courts of Chivalry.

As for the sheath of the blade, King Arthur lost it through the treachery of one who should by rights have been his dearest friend (as you will hear soon). In the end the loss of that miraculous sheath caused him a very great deal of pain and sorrow.
You will read about all of that, too, God willing, in due time.

So ends the story of the winning of Excalibur. May God grant you in your life that you may have His truth to help you, like a shining sword, to overcome your enemies. May He give you Faith (for Faith holds Truth as a scabbard holds its sword), and may that Faith heal all your wounds of sorrow as the sheath of Excalibur healed all the wounds of the one who wore that excellent weapon. For with Truth and Faith belted on, you will be as well able to fight all your battles as that noble hero of old, whom men called King Arthur.
